Search/fetch must be a tool because tools are the only MCP primitive that accepts parameters like a search query, and resources in MCP are limited to serving a single fixed, non-parameterized piece of content per URI.

Filing a bug report should be modeled as a prompt, since prompts are MCP's mechanism for triggering server-side actions and can be invoked by the client whenever a user-initiated action needs to run on the server.
questions.explanation: MCP's tools primitive is for model-invoked actions (here, filing a bug report has a clear side effect), while resources expose addressable, read-only data meant to be supplied as context - a closer match for searchable documentation content. Tools do accept parameters, so option C's reasoning is wrong; prompts are reusable prompt templates a server exposes to structure a client interaction, not a mechanism for performing actions, which rules out D.

questions.text: A team building on the Claude Agent SDK wants to give their agent a small set of custom tools (e.g., looking up internal feature flags) that only that one application will ever use. A developer proposes standing up a full external MCP server process communicating over stdio, configured in the same way a third-party MCP server would be. A teammate suggests defining the tools with the SDK's in-process MCP server helper (`createSdkMcpServer` and its associated tool-definition helper) instead. Which two statements accurately describe the tradeoff?
options: The in-process helper still presents the tools to the model through the same MCP tool-calling interface, but runs in the same process as the agent rather than requiring a separate subprocess to be spawned and managed - lower operational overhead for tools with no cross-application reuse need.

Standing up a full external stdio subprocess is justified here because it is the only way to give the tools proper JSON schema validation on their inputs, since in-process tool definitions skip schema validation entirely and pass whatever arguments the model produces straight through unchecked.

The in-process approach is a reasonable choice specifically because these tools are single-application and don't need to be independently deployed, versioned, or shared with other Claude applications - the reusability benefit of a standalone server isn't needed.

An external stdio MCP server subprocess is required whenever a tool needs to read local environment variables, since in-process tools run inside a sandboxed context that has no visibility into the host process's environment variables at all.

The two approaches are functionally identical in every respect, so the choice is purely a matter of code file organization and personal preference for where the tool-handling logic physically lives in the repository.
questions.explanation: The in-process SDK MCP server lets you define tools that plug into the same tool-calling interface without the overhead of managing a separate server process - the right tradeoff when a tool set is single-application and doesn't need independent deployment or cross-app reuse. JSON schema validation (B) isn't unique to external servers, and in-process code can read environment variables just as an external process can, so D is also false; the two approaches differ operationally (E is wrong to call them identical).

questions.text: A single internal analytics dashboard app needs Claude to compute a bespoke, app-specific risk score from fields already present in that app's request context. No other application will ever need this calculation, and it doesn't call out to any external system. What is the most appropriate way to expose this capability to Claude?
options: Build a dedicated MCP server for the risk-score calculation so it can be maintained and versioned independently, even though the calculation itself never needs to be reused outside this one dashboard application.

Define it as a custom tool local to this one application, since the logic is self-contained, has a single consumer, and gains nothing from the deployment and protocol overhead of a standalone MCP server.
Package it as an Agent Skill with bundled scripts, since any reusable capability should default to a Skill regardless of how small or single-purpose the underlying calculation actually is.

Rely on a built-in tool such as code execution to perform the calculation without defining any tool schema, since code execution can run arbitrary logic without Claude needing to know what the calculation does.
questions.explanation: A simple custom tool is the right level of infrastructure when a capability has exactly one consumer and no need for independent versioning or cross-application reuse - building an MCP server here (A) is the classic over-engineering trap, paying for reusability that will never be used. Skills (C) are suited to bundling instructions, scripts, and resources for a broader reusable workflow, not a single small in-app calculation; a built-in tool (D) doesn't apply since there is no general-purpose built-in capability for a bespoke, app-specific formula.

questions.text: A team needs Claude to call an internal inventory service exposed as a REST API. They want the capability to be reusable across several different Claude applications maintained by different teams, and updated independently of any one application's release cycle. Which approach best fits?
options: Hard-code the inventory operations into each application's system prompt so every team has full visibility into the logic, accepting that any change to the inventory service now has to be copied into every application's prompt separately.
Build an MCP server that exposes the inventory operations as tools, so multiple Claude applications can connect to the same server and it can be updated independently of any single app.

Paste a snapshot of current inventory levels into the context window on every request that might need it, so Claude always has the numbers available without waiting on a network call to the inventory service.

Rely on a built-in tool, since built-in tools can reach any internal REST API without additional configuration and would automatically pick up the inventory service's authentication and endpoint details.
questions.explanation: An MCP server is exactly the mechanism for exposing a capability that must be shared across multiple independent applications and maintained on its own release cycle. Hard-coding into prompts (A) is neither reusable nor independently maintainable; pasting a data snapshot (C) goes stale immediately and wastes context; built-in tools (D) don't have automatic access to arbitrary internal REST APIs.

questions.text: A finance team wants Claude to reliably produce quarterly variance reports: pull specific spreadsheet templates, apply a fixed sequence of formatting and calculation steps, and use several bundled reference scripts, all as a repeatable procedure invoked across many chat sessions. No external system needs to be called. Which approach is the best structural fit, over defining a handful of narrow custom tools for each step?
options: An Agent Skill, since it packages the instructions, reference files, and scripts for a specific reusable procedure into one invokable unit, rather than requiring Claude to correctly sequence several separate low-level tools every time.

An MCP server, since any reusable capability should be built as an MCP server regardless of whether it calls an external system, and standing up a server now would future-proof the workflow for other systems the finance team might integrate later on.

A single custom tool that accepts the entire request as one large free-text parameter and does everything internally in one opaque call, so Claude only needs to make one tool call per report instead of several.
A built-in tool, since spreadsheet manipulation is available out of the box in every Claude application and would already include the finance team's specific templates and formatting conventions.
questions.explanation: Skills are designed for exactly this shape: a reusable, multi-step procedure with bundled instructions and supporting files that Claude can invoke as a unit, without depending on any external service - which is what makes the MCP server option (B) unnecessary overhead here, since MCP's value is remote/shared-service integration, not local procedural bundling. A single opaque custom tool (C) sacrifices the model's ability to reason about and adapt intermediate steps, and no built-in tool provides this specific templated workflow (D).

questions.text: A support agent occasionally needs to look up current information from the public web to answer questions about a vendor's latest published pricing page. A developer proposes building a custom tool that scrapes the vendor's site via a bespoke HTTP client. What should be evaluated first?
options: Whether a built-in tool such as web search or web fetch already covers this need before investing in a custom scraper that must be independently maintained against site layout changes.
Whether to instead build a full MCP server around the custom scraper so it can be reused across other applications, without first checking if a built-in tool already solves the same need more simply.

Whether the custom scraper should be a client-side or server-side tool, moving straight to an implementation-placement decision without first asking whether a custom tool is the right approach at all.

Whether the vendor's pricing page content should be pasted into the system prompt permanently to avoid needing any tool, accepting that the number would only ever reflect whatever was true at the time it was copied in.
questions.explanation: The cheapest and most maintainable option should be ruled in or out first: a built-in web search/fetch tool already handles general public-web lookups without any custom code to maintain against site changes, so checking that is the correct first step before reaching for a custom build. Jumping to MCP-server reusability (B) or client/server placement (C) both skip past the more basic question of whether a custom tool is needed at all, and a static prompt paste (D) goes stale the moment pricing changes.

questions.text: A platform team is deciding, for two separate capabilities, between building an MCP server and building an Agent Skill. Capability 1: give several independent Claude applications, across different teams and infra, a live connection to a shared internal order-management system that changes data constantly. Capability 2: give Claude a consistent, repeatable procedure - with bundled checklist files and a formatting script - for writing internal incident postmortems, used only within one application. Select the two correct pairings.
options: Capability 1 is better served by an MCP server, since it needs a live, shared, cross-application connection to an external system of record.
Capability 1 is better served by a Skill, since Skills can bundle scripts that call external systems just as well as an MCP server can.
Capability 2 is better served by a Skill, since it's a self-contained, bundled procedure used within a single application with no live external system to connect to.
Capability 2 is better served by an MCP server, since any procedure involving files and scripts must be exposed as MCP resources.
Both capabilities are equally well served by either approach, since MCP servers and Skills are interchangeable packaging formats for the same underlying idea.
questions.explanation: MCP is the right fit when the defining need is a live, shared connection to an external, constantly-changing system reachable by multiple independent applications (Capability 1); a Skill is the right fit for a bundled, repeatable procedure with supporting files and scripts used inside one application with no external system in the loop (Capability 2). Option B is the half-right trap - it correctly notes Skills can run scripts, but that doesn't make them a substitute for a live multi-application connection to a changing external system, which is the actual requirement of Capability 1.

questions.text: A developer productivity platform serving several internal Claude-powered apps needs four capabilities: (a) run a generic public web search, (b) query a shared internal deployment-status service used by every team's app, (c) apply one team's own narrow, single-app helper that formats a commit message from a diff, with no external calls, (d) execute a documented, multi-step, bundled procedure for scaffolding a new internal microservice from templates, used repeatedly within one app. Select the two capability-to-approach pairings that are correct.
options: (a) should use a built-in web search tool rather than a custom-built scraper, since that capability is already covered out of the box.
(b) should be a custom tool defined separately inside each team's application, since duplicating the integration in every app guarantees each team stays in sync with the service's changes.
(c) should be a small custom tool local to that one application, since the logic is self-contained, single-consumer, and has no external call or cross-app reuse need.
(d) should be built as an MCP server, since any multi-step procedure with bundled templates must be exposed over MCP to be considered reusable.
(b) should be a built-in tool, since built-in tools can reach any internal company service without configuration.
questions.explanation: Public web search is exactly what a built-in tool already covers (a), and a self-contained, single-app, no-external-call helper like commit-message formatting is exactly the case for a lightweight custom tool (c) rather than heavier infrastructure. The trap is (b) framed as duplicated custom tools per app - duplicating an integration to a shared, constantly-changing service across every consuming app is precisely the maintenance burden an MCP server exists to avoid, since one server can be updated once for every app to reuse; built-in tools also don't have automatic access to arbitrary internal services (ruling out the second (b) option too). Capability (d) is a self-contained bundled procedure within a single app, which fits a Skill, not an MCP server - MCP is not a requirement for reusability, and Skills fill exactly this role.
